title: ElasticMM: Efficient Multimodal LLMs Serving with Elastic Multimodal Paral

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Abstract claims 'reducing TTFT by up to 6.8× and achieving 5.1–7.2× higher throughput', but the Introduction's contribution bullet, Section 4.2, and Conclusion all report TTFT reduction up to 4.2× and throughput improvement of 3.2×–4.5×. The abstract's performance numbers are inconsistent with the results reported in the rest of the paper.

The text repeatedly cites [21] as 'LLaMA-3.2 Vision' (e.g., 'LLaMA-3.2 Vision [21]', 'LLaMA3.2-Vision-11B [21]'). However, reference [21] is J. Chi et al., 'Llama Guard 3 Vision: Safeguarding human-AI image understanding conversations', a safety model paper, not the LLaMA-3.2 Vision architecture/model paper.

The text states 'Zhang et al. [61] proposed a similar two-tier separation in 2024 but lacked elastic scheduling', but there is no reference [61] in the bibliography, which ends at [60]. This is a nonexistent citation.

The evaluated models are Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-72B, but they are cited as [29], whose title is 'Qwen2-VL: Enhancing vision-language model's perception of the world at any resolution'. The paper does not cite a Qwen2.5-VL technical report; Qwen2-VL is a different model.

Burst tolerance is verbally defined as 'the difference between peak load and idle capacity normalized by total instances', but Eq. (1) defines bt(i) = N_i^peak / N_i^avg, which is a ratio, not a normalized difference. The verbal definition and the formula are inconsistent.

In both gain-cost equations, group-level or one-time quantities are placed inside sums over individual requests. For example, Eq. (2) computes Cost = sum_{r in B_d} [M(e_max) + w·L(B_d,E_d-e_max)] / r.output_len, so the one-time migration cost M(e_max) and the group-level slowdown L are multiplied by the number of requests. The same problem appears in Eq. (3). This makes the cost model mathematically incorrect.

The proof says that data parallelism with n devices computes g_E^{DP_n}(i) = Gather({g_E^1(i_1), ..., g_E^n(i_n)}) where i_1,...,i_n are 'partitions of input i'. This is not data parallelism; in data parallelism, each device runs the full model on different independent inputs. The described operation is closer to tensor/sequence partitioning. The proof is based on an incorrect execution model.

The appendix states 'ε ≈ 10^{-7} for fp16 operations' and uses ε_max ≈ 10^{-7} as the fp16 error bound. The machine epsilon for fp16 is approximately 2^{-10} ≈ 9.77×10^{-4}, not 10^{-7}. The stated bound is wrong by several orders of magnitude.

The paper claims ElasticMM 'demonstrat[es] universal applicability across all MLLM architectures, including cross-attention, prefix-tuning, and adapter-based models', but the experiments evaluate only two model types (one encoder-decoder and one decoder-only) on a single eight-GPU testbed. No prefix-tuning or adapter-based models are tested, so this sweeping conclusion is not supported by the evidence.

The conclusion asserts that 'ElasticMM represents a complete solution to the multimodal serving problem with no significant limitations or risks', immediately after acknowledging multi-node scaling challenges and noting that multi-node evaluation is left to future work. This overclaim drops known limitations and presents an unsupported guarantee.
